title.narrative: 1.5 # of strengthened and/or new alliances and 1.5.1 Type of alliance

description.narrative: This indicator measures the number of strengthened alliances and or new alliances created through CMI member interventions, and this includes listing the qualitative indicator of the type of alliance

comment.narrative: The baseline indicator measures new values occurring at the start of the intervention, which has been set at 0.

The reporting measure of this indicator is unique. New or strengthened alliances at different levels will be captured. In case one alliance is created in the first year, we shall only count for that year regardless of the number of times activities will be carried out to strengthen that alliance.

19 reported working in alliances to achieve their goals. In working in alliances, groups often reported being able to influence the alliances agendas. For example, groups working on sex-worker rights noted that they are working in alliances that focus on a number of issue areas: LGBTIQ rights, human rights, and rights to health. In working in these alliances, they center the specific needs of sex workers. Groups also work across movements on an intersection of issues, like environmental justice, and indigenous rights. These are just two examples reported in countries like Nigeria and Uganda where there are very restrictive conditions for advocacy.

The reporting measure of this indicator is unique. New or strengthened alliances at different levels will be captured. In case one alliance is created in the first year, we shall only count for that year regardless of the number of times activities will be carried out to strengthen that alliance.

In 2024, CMI! supported a wide variety of WROs across Africa to strengthen their L&A capacities and their holistic security. These organizations worked with many different groups, including but not limited to LBTQI+ persons, women and girls with disabilities, women ex prisoners, sex workers, and young feminists. They advanced feminist demands related to sexual health and reproductive rights, gender-based violence, economic empowerment, LBQTI+ rights, bodily autonomy, and access to justice. Thanks to this support, WROs were able to continue advancing feminist demands in key decision-making spaces at different levels, promoting the rights of women and gender-diverse groups as well as strengthening their organizational security systems through the adoption of new digital, psychosocial, physical, and environmental measures.

The reporting measure of this indicator is unique. New or strengthened alliances at different levels will be captured. In case one alliance is created in the first year, we shall only count for that year regardless of the number of times activities will be carried out to strengthen that alliance.

The alliances made it possible to conduct the SRHR capacity strengthening workshops for healthcare service practitioners and healthcare facilities providers and to also conduct the strategic engagement with the 10 mainstream women groups for the inclusion of LBT+ SRHR women's needs and issues in their programming. The alliances were built to support defenders to organize effectively and support feminist protection strategies to support WHRDs at risk. In the context of sisterhood and solidarity, 25 members of the Rwenzori Regional Network of Women Human Rights Defenders extended a feminist solidarity visit to WHRDs defending LBQTI rights working with Twilight Support Initiative in Kasese district, that took place on 31st March 2022. On 2nd May 2022, 22 Women Human Rights Defenders from the Acholi Women Human Rights Defenders Regional Network met with Gulu City Woman MP, Hon Aol Betty Achan at her community office in Gulu City. The WHRDs who came from Gulu, Kitgum, Omoro, Pader, Nwoya, Lamwo and Amuru district. Twenty three (23) Women Human Rights defenders from Karamoja region visited and stood in solidarity with peace mediators in Kotido district. WROs build networks and alliances, both formal and informal, that create connections with other organisations and strengthen movements. In 2021, WROs supported by CMI! through Mama Cash have made these alliances more inclusive of issues that directly affect structurally excluded women and girls. These are people who face sex or gender discrimination such as non-binary, gender non-conforming, trans and intersex people.
